title.en: Izu Oshima: an island and its ferries
title.ja: 伊豆大島：島の経済とフェリー

summary.en: A volcanic island of about 6,800 people, 1h45m from Tokyo by jet ferry. Visitors, inns, shops, fishers, young islanders and the ferry operator all react to each other, week by week.
summary.ja: 人口 約 6,800 人の火山の島。東京からジェット船で 1 時間 45 分。観光客、宿、店、漁師、島の若者、船会社が、1 週間ごとにお互いに反応し合う。

scenario.en: Model the economy of Izu Oshima, a small island near Tokyo, week by week: visitors arriving by jet ferry and large ship, inns, restaurants and shops, fishing and farming, jobs, and population. First reproduce today's situation, then test events such as adding ferry sailings: does it pay for the operator, and does it revive the island?
scenario.ja: 東京に近い小さな島、伊豆大島の経済を 1 週間ごとにモデル化してほしい。ジェット船と大型客船で来る観光客、宿、飲食店と商店、漁業と農業、仕事、人口を扱う。まず今の状況を再現し、そのあと「フェリーの本数を増やす」などの事件を試したい。船会社は元が取れるか、島は活性化するか。

questions.en: If the jet ferry runs more often, does the route still make money?
questions.ja: ジェット船を増やしても、航路は黒字のままか。

questions.en: Do more sailings bring more visitors, jobs and residents, or just emptier boats?
questions.ja: 本数を増やすと、観光客・仕事・住民は増えるのか。空席が増えるだけか。

questions.en: What stops the island from growing first: seats, beds, or workers?
questions.ja: 島の成長を最初に止めるのは何か。座席か、ベッドか、働き手か。

assumptions.en: Population and ferry fares come from public pages. Visitor numbers, ferry costs, seats, beds, wages and all elasticities are assumptions and need checking.
assumptions.ja: 人口と運賃は公開されている数字。来島者数、船の費用、座席数、ベッド数、賃金、弾力性はすべて仮定で、要確認。

assumptions.en: Each visitor pays the fare twice (round trip). The operator keeps about 80% of the list fare after discounts.
assumptions.ja: 来島者は運賃を 2 回払う（往復）。割引があるので、船会社の取り分は定価の約 80% とする。

assumptions.en: The ferry profit covers this route only and ignores the rest of the company.
assumptions.ja: フェリーの損益はこの航路だけの計算で、会社全体は見ていない。

agents.persona: The route manager of the ferry company that serves the island. Must keep the route profitable over the year, knows that jet ferries burn a lot of fuel, and is wary of adding sailings that run half empty outside the peak season. Also feels a duty to the islanders who depend on the boats.
Owners of small family inns and a few hotels. Many are over 60 with no successor. They invest only when they have seen full rooms for a while, and they fear debt. A few younger owners are ambitious.

Owners of restaurants, souvenir shops, rental and diving businesses. Income swings wildly between summer and winter. Finding staff is hard. They like island fish and vegetables but mainland wholesale is cheaper and more reliable.
Fishers and growers of camellia and ashitaba. Ageing, proud of their produce. Tokyo markets pay better but shipping depends on the large ship and the weather. Steady local buyers are valued.
Islanders aged 18 to 35. They love the island but want a stable job, friends of their own age, and easy trips to Tokyo. Many compare island wages with what classmates earn in the city.
Mainland people, often remote workers or couples in their 30s, who dream of island life. They need a job or reliable internet, a house, and a way to reach Tokyo for work several times a month.

Tokyo-area people looking for a one-day outing. They compare the island with Kamakura, Atami or Hakone. A day trip only works if a morning boat goes out and an afternoon boat comes back; the fare is the main cost.

name.ja: 週末のカップル・家族

agents.persona: Couples and families planning a one or two night trip. They book a few weeks ahead, want a comfortable inn and good food, and give up quickly if boats or rooms are full on the dates they want.

name.ja: ダイバー・登山客・サイクリスト

agents.persona: Divers, Mount Mihara hikers and cyclists. Loyal repeat visitors who care more about conditions than price, stay two nights, and often take the cheaper overnight ship.
Organised tours of older travellers and school groups. Booked months ahead by agencies that need guaranteed seats and beds in blocks; they avoid the island when capacity looks tight.
The town's planning section chief. Small budget, council pressure to stop population decline, and a cautious habit of doing one measure at a time.
